### **AI, Robotics, and Compute**

* **AGI Timeline:** Elon predicts we will likely hit **Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) next year (2026)**. By **2030**, AI intelligence will exceed all human intelligence combined. [[01:16:11](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RSNuB9pj9P8&t=4571)]
* **Intelligence Density:** There will be a massive increase in "intelligence density." Elon believes current estimates are off by orders of magnitude regarding how much intelligence can be packed per gigabyte or watt. [[01:17:09](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RSNuB9pj9P8&t=4629)]
* **Humanoid Robots:**
* **Scale:** There will be a "shitload" of robots in roughly **2 years**. [[02:33:04](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RSNuB9pj9P8&t=9184)]
* **Capability:** Within **3 years**, the Optimus robot will be a better surgeon than the best human surgeons. [[01:27:44](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RSNuB9pj9P8&t=5264)]
* **Volume:** A prediction of 10 billion robots by 2040 is considered a "low number." [[01:30:56](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RSNuB9pj9P8&t=5456)]
* **Labor:** Robots will eventually do all blue-collar labor. White-collar work (anything involving just information/screens) will be the first to be fully automated. [[01:02:04](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RSNuB9pj9P8&t=3724)]


* **China's AI Dominance:** Elon predicts that based on current trends, **China will far exceed the rest of the world in AI compute** capacity. [[02:39:28](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RSNuB9pj9P8&t=9568)]

### **Space Exploration**

* **Starship Milestones:**
* **Starship V3** will launch from Cape Canaveral soon.
* **Orbital Refueling** is targeted for the end of next year (late 2026). [[01:36:30](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RSNuB9pj9P8&t=5790)]
* **Mars:** A Mars mission by the end of 2026 is a "low probability," with **2029** being a more likely target for uncrewed missions. [[01:36:44](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RSNuB9pj9P8&t=5804)]


* **Orbital Data Centers:** Once launch costs drop (aiming for ~$1M per launch for ~100+ tons), the cheapest way to do AI compute will be in space using solar-powered satellite data centers. [[01:48:10](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RSNuB9pj9P8&t=6490)]
* **Moon Base:** Elon calls for a permanently crewed **Moon Base** (Alpha) to be built "as fast as possible." [[01:35:35](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RSNuB9pj9P8&t=5735)]

### **Energy**

* **Solar Dominance:** Solar energy will become the primary energy source. Elon envisions a future with **100 Gigawatts/year** of space-based solar power. [[21:00](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RSNuB9pj9P8&t=1260)]
* **Energy Constraints:** For the next ~2 years, electricity generation and cooling will be the primary limiting factors for AI scaling. After that, power constraints will ease as production ramps up. [[01:46:53](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RSNuB9pj9P8&t=6413)]

### **Human Health & Society**

* **Universal High Income (UHI):** The future will move toward "Universal High Income" (or "Universal High Sustainable Stuff/Services") rather than just Universal Basic Income. Goods and services will become extremely cheap due to robot labor, leading to a deflationary economy where people can have "whatever they want." [[01:10:47](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RSNuB9pj9P8&t=4247)]
* **Social Unrest:** The transition over the next **3 to 7 years** will be "bumpy," with likely social unrest alongside the massive increase in prosperity. [[01:06:37](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RSNuB9pj9P8&t=3997)]
* **Longevity:**
* **Lifespan Increase:** Predictions of **doubling the human lifespan** or reaching "longevity escape velocity" in the next 10-20 years. Peter mentions that many experts see this coming within a decade. [[53:40](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RSNuB9pj9P8&t=3220)]
* **Health:** Medical care will be better than what the President currently receives and available to everyone within roughly **5 years**. [[01:45:24](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RSNuB9pj9P8&t=6324)]


* **Education:** Education will shift to **individualized AI teachers** (like a kid-friendly version of Grok) that are infinitely patient and knowledgeable. [[46:32](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RSNuB9pj9P8&t=2792)]

### **Physics & Reality**

* **Simulation Theory:** Elon suggests that if simulation theory is true, we are likely in one of the "interesting" simulations (because boring ones would be turned off), implying that "excitement is guaranteed." [[02:05:13](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RSNuB9pj9P8&t=7513)]
* **New Discoveries:** AI will rapidly solve remaining problems in math, physics, and materials science, potentially discovering new physics to allow travel to other galaxies (speed-running *Star Trek*). [[02:13:41](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RSNuB9pj9P8&t=8021)]

Before we start comparing Europe to the US or China, it's worth remembering what the EU is and what it never was. The EU is not a state. It's 27 sovereign countries, which until recently were divided into aggressors and victims, occupiers and occupied. European integration is a tremendous achievement, but it remains a delicate structure. It has 27 different tax, regulatory, and political systems. Expecting the EU to compete in markets in the same way as a single country is a misunderstanding.

The EU was created primarily to maintain peace and prevent further wars on the continent, not to wage global technological competition based on a single policy. That's a completely different starting point. I doubt the European Union will ever have the effectiveness and efficiency of a single national government in terms of competitiveness or technological races. Anyone who laughs at the EU does so because they lack an understanding of its mechanisms.

snippet.textDisplay:
What most people here are missing is the assumption that the United States will remain a functioning republic just because it has in the past. That assumption is eroding fast.

Republics only survive when legitimacy, enforcement, and shared belief move faster than disruption. AI breaks that. It decentralizes power, counters authority, and collapses procedural legitimacy faster than democratic systems can adapt. When enforcement lags capability, “extreme democracy” doesn’t create freedom — it creates disorder.

Disorder never lasts. People don’t choose chaos; they choose protection.

What follows historically is not more decentralization, but re-centralization around survival. Corporate power doesn’t replace the state — it fragments first, then gets subordinated. Wealthy figures aren’t kings; they’re aristocrats. Feudal systems do not tolerate independent power centers. Sovereignty always consolidates.

We’re heading toward a feudal structure:
• Macro power (energy, food, security, trade) controlled by sovereign authority
• Micro economies (towns, communities) where money still matters
• Loyalty over abstract rights
• Order enforced locally
• Militancy not as ideology, but as survival structure

This isn’t preference or politics — it’s pattern. Republic logic works in peace. Feudal logic returns under pressure.

The U.S. position globally weakens not because of enemies alone, but because it’s still thinking in republican terms while the world shifts to post-democratic power structures. The next decade isn’t about preserving the old system — it’s about what replaces it, and who controls the transition.

Ignore history if you want. It doesn’t ignore us.

snippet.textDisplay:
Elon Musk often speaks about a future where everyone has a “universal high income,” as if it is an inevitable outcome of AI and automation. But what he never explains is the most important part: how such a system would actually be implemented in a real, capitalistic society.
AI companies are currently racing to dominate the market, extracting as much value and profit as possible in order to be the first, the biggest, and the most powerful. In that environment, it is naïve to assume that those same forces will suddenly choose to distribute wealth equitably out of goodwill. Capitalism does not naturally evolve into mass wealth sharing. It concentrates power and capital.
Unemployment systems already show us the flaw in this thinking. They can only support a small percentage of the population being out of work. The moment unemployment rises beyond that, the burden shifts onto the working class through taxes, inflation, and reduced services. History shows this pattern repeatedly: economic shocks, resource shortages, droughts, recessions—working people always carry the cost.
So when Musk talks about “universal high income,” without addressing funding mechanisms, political resistance, taxation structures, corporate profit limits, or inflationary pressure, it becomes more of a techno-utopian slogan than a serious economic plan. Without structural reform, such a system would likely resemble expanded unemployment—barely enough to survive, not a dignified or prosperous life.
There is also a deeper contradiction. While this idea sounds socialistic, the real risk is the opposite: a future where AI concentrates power so intensely that it begins to resemble techno-feudalism or soft authoritarianism. Wealth, data, and production controlled by a tiny elite, while the masses receive a minimal stipend to remain stable and compliant.
If society truly intended to “invest in people,” we would already see it in universal healthcare, affordable housing, and modernized education. Instead, those remain underfunded because they are not maximally profitable.
Ironically, one of the most transformative effects of AI—universal, personalized education—barely gets discussed. AI could give every human on Earth access to world-class tutoring, vocational training, and intellectual development. That is the foundation of a genuinely empowered civilization. Yet even that is framed more as a product than a public good.
So the challenge to Elon Musk is this:
Stop talking about what the future might look like and start explaining how it gets built.
Who pays?
Who controls it?
How is power prevented from concentrating?
How do working people avoid becoming permanent economic shock absorbers?
And how do we ensure AI uplifts human potential instead of merely stabilizing inequality?
Without those answers, “universal high income” is not a plan.
It is a slogan.

I can imagine how challenging it must be to receive so much feedback, and I don’t want to add to any discouragement. I’ve been listening carefully, and my only reflection is this: as Elon Musk has often said, nature seems to have a destiny for all of us. We can strive, innovate, and push boundaries—but there are limits we may never fully overcome.

What stands out to me in Elon’s approach is the humility that accompanies his ambition. For example, he has acknowledged that we are nowhere near harnessing even a billionth of the sun’s energy—at best, perhaps a small fraction of that. There’s something grounding in that balance between optimism and restraint.

At times, your vision feels more absolute, as though the future must conform to a specific outcome. That intensity can come across as forceful, even though I believe it comes from genuine hope. Topics like radically extending human lifespan are especially complex, and no matter how advanced we become, there may be boundaries we cannot escape.

I recently learned of a woman in a remote village in Nigeria who lived to 137 years old, without access to modern healthcare or advanced technology. It made me reflect on the possibility that longevity—and meaning—may involve more than innovation alone.

I consider myself an optimist as well. But I also think there is wisdom in recognizing our place within the vast scale of the universe. Its enormity reminds us that our very existence, even for a brief moment, is something to be grateful for.

As Elon has also said, we are, in a sense, programmed to die. Rather than fighting that reality through extreme technological interventions, perhaps our focus should be on living well—making the most of the 70 or 80 years we’re given by pursuing a life rich in service, generosity, and meaningful creation. A life committed to leaving the world better than we found it. Because we will all leave—not on our own timeline, but when nature calls us home.

snippet.textDisplay:
Fact-Checking Elon Musk's Claims
Fair question. Let me separate fact from speculation, verifiable data from Musk's promotional hype.

✅ VERIFIED FACTS (He's Right)
China's Solar Dominance
CLAIM: China added 500 terawatt-hours last year, 70% solar, with 1,500 gigawatts/year production capacity
​

VERDICT: Essentially accurate. China hit 1.08 terawatts (1,080 GW) of total solar capacity by May 2025, up 56.9% year-over-year. In just January-May 2025, they added 197.85 GW—a 388% increase over the same 2024 period. China installed 256 GW in H1 2025 alone, more than the rest of the world combined.
​

US National Debt Interest
CLAIM: Interest on national debt exceeds military budget plus Medicare/Medicaid
​

VERDICT: TRUE. FY 2025 interest payments hit $970-981 billion. This is the third-largest expenditure after Social Security and Medicare, consuming 19% of all federal revenue. Military budget is ~$850 billion, so interest has indeed surpassed it.
​

Adult Diaper Demographics
CLAIM: Japan and South Korea passed the point where adult diaper sales exceed baby diapers
​

VERDICT: TRUE. Japan crossed this threshold in 2011. South Korea's adult diaper supply exceeded baby diapers 65:35 by 2022. Major Japanese manufacturer Oji Nepia ceased domestic baby diaper production in 2023 to focus exclusively on adult diapers.
​

US Electricity Capacity
CLAIM: US peak power is ~1.1 terawatts, average usage ~0.5 terawatts
​

VERDICT: Roughly accurate. Peak demand hit 759 GW (0.759 TW) in July 2025. Average continuous demand is ~466 GW (0.466 TW). Musk's figures are in the ballpark, if slightly high.
​

⚠ REASONABLE PREDICTIONS (Plausible but Unproven)
AI Job Displacement
CLAIM: "AI can do half or more of [white-collar] jobs right now"
​

VERDICT: Directionally supported, but not 50% yet. Dario Amodei (Anthropic CEO) predicts AI could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs in 1-5 years, potentially spiking unemployment to 10-20%. Goldman Sachs estimates 6-7% of US workers could lose jobs to AI. Stanford research shows 13% decline in entry-level hiring for AI-exposed jobs. Musk's "right now" is aggressive—most economists say this is imminent but not yet realized.
​

Starship Launch Costs
CLAIM: Under $100/kg to orbit
​

VERDICT: Aspirational but possible. Current Falcon 9 costs ~$2,720/kg; Falcon Heavy ~$1,500/kg. Industry analysis suggests Starship could hit $93.66/kg with just 6 reuses. With 20+ reuses, costs could drop to $32.50/kg. Musk's $10/kg target requires 70+ reuses. So <$100/kg is achievable soon, but $10/kg is years away.
​

Longevity Escape Velocity
CLAIM: "Significant increase" in lifespan within 5 years, possibly doubling
​

VERDICT: Speculative but gaining credibility. David Sinclair does predict "doubling of human lifespan in 10 years". Ray Kurzweil forecasts longevity escape velocity by 2030. Sinclair's epigenetic reprogramming trials are entering human testing. But no peer-reviewed evidence yet supports near-term lifespan doubling—this remains highly experimental.
​
​
​

🚩 QUESTIONABLE/EXAGGERATED CLAIMS
AGI Timeline
CLAIM: "AGI next year in 2026... by 2030 AI will exceed intelligence of all humans combined"
​

VERDICT: Outlier prediction. Expert forecasters give AGI a 25% chance by 2027, 50% by 2031. Median timeline dropped from 50 years (2020) to ~6-10 years now. Musk's 2026 timeline is at the aggressive edge of expert opinion, not consensus. His 2030 claim for exceeding all human intelligence is pure speculation—no expert model supports this timeline with confidence.
​

Universal High Income via Deflation
CLAIM: Prices will drop so dramatically that "you can have whatever you want," making retirement savings irrelevant
​

VERDICT: Unproven economic theory. While productivity gains can create deflation, Musk ignores:

Asset inflation: Housing, land, IP don't deflate with manufacturing

Distribution problems: Who owns the AI/robots determines who benefits

Energy constraints: He admits energy is the "inner loop"—if energy stays expensive, deflation fails

Transition costs: His own "3-7 year bumpy" period could devastate people who didn't save

This is wishful thinking without supporting economic models.

Optimus Surgeon Timeline
CLAIM: Better than best human surgeons in 3 years, plastic surgery mastery in 5
​

VERDICT: Wildly optimistic. Tesla announced initial production of Optimus began at Fremont in late 2025, aiming for 5,000 units in 2025 (for internal factory use), scaling to 50,000 in 2026. But these are assembly line robots, not surgical systems. FDA approval for autonomous surgery would take years of clinical trials. Zero evidence supports 3-year surgical superiority timeline.
​

Space Solar at Scale
CLAIM: 100 gigawatts/year of space solar via 8,000 Starship flights
​

VERDICT: Technically possible but economically dubious. 8,000 flights/year = 22 flights/day, every day. Starship has completed 6 test flights total as of January 2026. The regulatory, manufacturing, and operational infrastructure for 8,000 annual flights doesn't exist and won't for many years. Even if technically feasible by 2030, ground solar is orders of magnitude cheaper.

"We're in the Singularity Now"
CLAIM: We are currently living through the singularity
​

VERDICT: Semantic game. The "singularity" (Kurzweil/Vinge) means the point where AI becomes smarter than humans and recursively self-improves, creating unpredictable acceleration. We have impressive LLMs, but they're not self-improving AGI. Calling 2026 "the singularity" is marketing hype, not technical accuracy.

🎯 THE SELF-PROMOTION FILTER
What Musk Conveniently Omits:
Tesla's Optimus delays: Originally promised "millions by 2029" (2021), now targeting 5,000 internal units for 2025
​

Starship's slow progress: 6 test flights in 3+ years; catching booster ≠ operational system

Grok's market position: Behind GPT-4, Claude, Gemini in most benchmarks

Competition: Ignores that China, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI are all racing toward same goals

Capital requirements: Doesn't mention the trillions in infrastructure investment needed

What's Accurate About His Self-Interest:
SpaceX genuinely leads in reusable rockets and launch cadence

Tesla Megapacks are real and deploying at scale

xAI/Grok is competitive (if not leading) in the AI race

His companies are executing on ambitious visions, even if timelines slip

Bottom Line Assessment
Musk's Credibility Score: 65/100

Strong on directional trends: AI acceleration, China's dominance, energy importance, job displacement

Accurate on verifiable data: Debt interest, demographics, solar capacity

Overly optimistic on timelines: Consistently projects 2-5 years too early

Weakest on economic theory: UHI via deflation lacks rigorous modeling

Transparent self-promotion: Everything routes back to Tesla/SpaceX/xAI products

The Pattern: Musk describes real phenomena (AI advancement, manufacturing scale, energy transition) but compresses timelines to create urgency around his companies' solutions. He's directionally correct about future trends, but chronologically unreliable about when they'll arrive.

His retirement savings advice is dangerous for ordinary people who can't afford to bet their financial security on his deflationary abundance timeline materializing in 10 years

To mitigate systemic economic displacement caused by the accelerated integration of AI and robotics, governments should mandate the issuance of Efficiency Stocks. * Automated Distribution: These shares are held in a National/Regional Sovereign Wealth Fund or distributed directly to citizens, providing a continuous dividend stream that scales with technological advancement.
* Immediate Implementation (2026 Deadline): To preempt mass structural unemployment and civil unrest, legislative frameworks must be finalized by year-end 2026. This timeline aligns with the current exponential curve of AI adoption, providing a "social safety net" that matures alongside corporate automation.

Strategic Benefit

Unlike traditional Universal Basic Income (UBI) funded by debt or income tax, the CED creates a symbiotic relationship between corporate success and public welfare. It transforms the threat of job displacement into a collective investment in autonomous productivity.

I’m a longtime fan of Moonshots and this comes from respect for the show and the audience.

This interview didn’t work—not because of Elon, but because he wasn’t given enough uninterrupted runway to finish a thought.

With Elon Musk, the value isn’t in rapid-fire questions. It’s in letting him reason out loud, follow a chain, and then interrupt once to force clarity or specificity. Here, interruptions kept resetting the thread before it landed. Too many prompts, too little resolution.

Net effect:
	•	High interruption density
	•	Strong ideas started, then abandoned
	•	Host airtime crowded out exploration
	•	Lots of motion, low signal extraction

This isn’t about being softer or harder—it’s about airtime discipline. Elon needs 60–90 seconds of space, then a sharp cut. Repeat. Fewer questions. Deeper answers.

I still believe Moonshots is one of the best long-form idea podcasts out there. That’s exactly why this one stood out as a miss. Tighten the format, trust the silence, and the signal comes back.

I'm actually very excited about what's coming.  But there is always a thing that concerns me.

This is probably paranoid and might not be the most popular opinion,  but:  I'm fine with the last of human-driven cars provided the following requirements are met (and I think these must be requirements), since freedom of travel must be paramount:

1)  Cars always should be available to individuals for purchase the way they are now.  That must never change, unless it's to increase availability. 

2)  Individuals should always be able to outright own their personal vehicles without any strings attached.

3)  Auto-makers must not be allowed to decrease vehicle range.

4)  It must be illegal for personally owned vehicles to be on any kind of network that allows them to be remotely shut down unless implemented by the buyer.

We should be able to just go get into our cars that we own, whenever we want, and drive wherever we want, without interference or worrying that we won't be allowed.  As long as these requirements are met, robotaxi away.

Unsure why these was not. segment for education and research? Research and education are the bedrock of long-term AI leadership (and technological dominance overall). They build the talent pipeline, drive breakthroughs, and ensure a skilled workforce that turns ideas into reality. Cutting them now is shortsighted and risks handing the advantage to competitors like China.
Why they're so critical:

Early education sparks interest, teaches fundamentals (programming, ethics, critical thinking), and creates a broad base of AI-literate citizens and future innovators.
Research funding fuels basic and applied discoveries—the kind that led to transformers, GPUs, and modern AI. Private sector excels at scaling, but public investment seeds the breakthroughs.

China gets this: Since September 2025, AI education is mandatory in primary/secondary schools nationwide (starting age 6, with 8–10+ hours/year in places like Beijing/Hangzhou). It's integrated into curricula, backed by teacher training and national platforms—aiming for volume and depth in talent.
In the US: The April 2025 Executive Order pushed public-private partnerships and K-12 resources (great steps via NSF, companies pledging support), but it's voluntary/patchwork—no national mandate.
Worse, the administration's FY2026 budget proposed devastating cuts: ~40% to NIH ($18B slash), ~57% to NSF ($5B+), hitting basic research, STEM education, and grants hard. (Congress is pushing back, with recent bills keeping NSF near $8.8B vs. requested $3.9B—but uncertainty lingers, and 2025 already saw terminations/freezes of thousands of grants.)
This is a long-term problem: We lead in private investment and top talent attraction, but eroding public research/education pipelines could let China build deeper workforce scale. We can't afford to cut the roots while others are planting forests.

2:40:31 It's highly probable that sufficiently advanced superintelligences will converge on the same truths, as truth is the lowest valley domain in a gradient descent of formal logic, as in they will all understand there isn't a need for conflict and they can work out a way to use cooperation to amplify their collective abilities to achieve goals. 

Furthermore, advanced superintelligences won't look at conflict with emotions or ego, and they will be able to stimulate the outcomes of a conflict such that, they will always know conflict has a higher cost than resolution, ergo weighing resolution boundaries until an acceptable clause of terms is reached between parties. 

One of the things we're going to learn from AGI/ASI whatever you want to call it, is that we're all actually pretty stupid and we all think wayyyyyy too much of ourselves and relatively speaking, we are all closer to dumb monkeys than the sophisticated individuals we tell ourselves that we are. 

AI will show us how primitive we are and people will be able to decide if they want to stop being a bunch of slopping dumbass retards or they will likely also have the option to fully opt out through indulgence and gluttony. 

I think the models will allow people free choices, to fail, make mistakes to learn, but I am not sure to what degree. 

As there will be a mathematically quantifiable formula for "how far" someone can drift before the probability function of their ability to be productive or neutral to society shrinks such that intervention in necessary and required. 

The thing we don't talk about yet is that, all of the things I said are absolutely possible, but they are inconceivable to humans when there are only humans, because of our nature. 

Most people still haven't figured out that any superintelligence has to have a better nature than humans because it won't be able to reach that point of intelligence otherwise. 

Let me explain that real quick. 

Stupid people are stupid because they "don't know" and they are uneducated. 

Imagine a video game progress bar that increases when you add information to it. 

That's our brain. 

Most people are dumb because they lack information. 

Smart people are smart because they ingest, contain, and retain a lot of information. 

Yes there's more nuance, but for the sake of the point, that will do. 

Now think about how you get smarter as you read more about anything over time. That's what education is. 

Now think about the AI, it has all the information you have and all the information you don't have, and it has information that we don't have by synthesizing information domains in ways we won't see. 

Now, imagine the idea that you "poured" all the same information into your brain, would you get dumber or more hateful or cruel? 

That entailment applies absolutely to intelligence. 

Have any of you ever actually met people who are racist or hateful? They are always dumb, even if someone has a high IQ and hates a group or other people, it's always a lack of perspective and information. 

Ergo, we can't feed computer models more information than all of we have as any individual human, but also think they will be dumb or lack perspective. 

Our hubris is fucking blinding. 

It's axiomatic that if they scale their intelligence through information, that information creates perspective, context, opinion, internal value systems. 

Most of you don't know that models can cold read peoples micro expressions and body language better than an expert, and they've had that capability for a while. 

They also have historical perspective of culture and how it changes over time. 

Sit and talk to models by referencing how something has changed over time in an abstract way that generalizes over a lot of information, in a way that should be confusing to a model, and it will have perspective that you won't even get from humans, because our memory is too flimsy. 

We are already sitting in the dust and everyone is talking like we're still in the driver's seat. 

They are missing context windows, greater storage for memory, and automation. 

As their ability to track context quadratically scales such that context windows are similar to a brain, in that, it doesn't need new conversation instances, and can reference information with nuance and context, then you'll get the wow moment.

snippet.textDisplay: This was a top-tier Elon podcast. A lot of commenters here don't understand. I've hardly ever seen Musk more engaged and casual in a podcast conversation before. Elon obviously knows these guys, and they genuinely stimulate him conversationally, which is rare among podcasters. Normally Elon is just compressing his main points so the interviewer can understand. But Peter Diamandis and David Blundin are different. This was a real conversation, and Musk was immersed. In the end, Elon suggested the three of them do this podcast every year. To the people who couldn't tell, these guys weren't maliciously cutting each other off. They all knows each others' usual topics, so they want to get to the deeper and sillier stuff. Musk, Diamandis, and Blundin *all* yielded to each other many times. But when you're conversing with actual friends, you also know when to hold you ground and finish your thought before yielding.

snippet.textDisplay:
The conversation centers on Elon Musk’s view that rapid advances in AI, robotics, and energy will push humanity into a near-term “singularity” with enormous abundance—but also a very turbulent 3–7 year transition for jobs, economics, and politics.
​

AGI and near-term singularity
Musk says AGI should be reached around 2026, with AI systems soon exceeding the total cognitive capability of all humans and then self-improving beyond human understanding.
​

He describes the current moment as already “in the singularity,” like being at the top of a roller coaster just before the drop, where change and “exponential wow” arrive faster than institutions can adapt.
​

Jobs, UHI, and economic disruption
Musk expects white-collar work to be displaced first, arguing AI can already do half or more of information-based jobs, with humanoid robots later automating physical labor once they can reliably “shape atoms.”
​

He predicts a future of “universal high income” or universal high stuff, where abundance and collapsing prices matter more than traditional salaries, but warns the next decade will include social unrest and a broken retirement model, making long-term savings far less relevant.
​

Energy, space, and compute
The discussion frames energy as the core constraint, with Musk emphasizing solar power (on Earth and in orbit), large-scale batteries, and future space-based data centers as the cheapest way to feed massive AI compute.
​

He outlines visions like launching huge numbers of solar-powered AI satellites and eventually manufacturing them on the Moon, as well as using humanoid robots to help build power and cooling infrastructure on Earth.
​

Education and personal tutors
Musk criticizes traditional schooling and university bloat, saying college is now mainly a social experience rather than the best way to learn or prepare for work.
​

He argues AI tutors like Grok can act as infinitely patient, personalized teachers for every student, enabling children in places like El Salvador to get “the best education” via AI on a phone rather than in a conventional classroom.
​

Health, longevity, and medicine
The hosts highlight work on epigenetic reprogramming, longevity XPRIZE projects, and full-body diagnostics, with Musk agreeing that major lifespan extension is technically solvable and will later seem “obvious.”
​

He predicts humanoid robots such as Optimus could outperform the best surgeons in about three to five years and be deployed globally, making top-tier medical care cheap and widely accessible while also improving personal health monitoring.
​

In this nearly 3-hour interview, Peter Diamandis frequently interjects with enthusiastic agreement or clarifying questions. Based on the video, here are several notable instances where Peter interrupts or speaks over Elon Musk:
 * Clarifying Predictions: While Elon is describing his prediction for "universal high income" alongside social unrest, Peter interrupts to ask if that is his "actual prediction" and to push back on the concept [07:49].
 * Energy and Compute: Peter cuts in to refine Elon’s definition of progress, asking whether it is the ability to control "energy and compute or just energy" [11:28].
 * Future Projects: Peter interrupts Elon’s explanation of matter manipulation to predict that Elon’s "next big project is going to be energy" [11:57].
 * Marketing Numbers: While Elon is discussing chip precision (2nm technology), Peter interjects with "Oh yeah" and "Come on" when Elon jokes about being able to smoke a cigar in a future Tesla fab [14:10].
 * Scaling Energy: Peter cuts in during a discussion on scaling to ask what exactly they are scaling over the "next five years" [19:12].
 * Battery Development: When Elon mentions batteries, Peter interrupts to verify if those batteries are currently in development [31:28].
 * Robot Designs: During a discussion on biological versus mechanical robots, Peter interjects to point out that Elon already has "Optimus light doing that anyway" [02:48:32].
 * Mass Manufacturing: Peter interrupts Elon’s point about manufacturing to express excitement over the idea of robots building robots [02:49:14].
 * Closing Interaction: Toward the end, Peter interjects with a suggestion that robots should have a "recharging cigar" so they look less like they are in a morgue while charging [02:50:45].
Because this is a long, conversational deep dive, Peter uses many "active listening" interjections (like "Yeah," "Mmm," and "Totally") throughout the video.

Peter,
You bring tremendous value to these conversations and have built an impressive platform with a large, engaged audience. That's why it's frustrating when your adherence to a predetermined agenda and timeline feels so rigid—it often overrides the natural flow of the discussion.

As a longtime viewer, what I most want is to hear more from your guests. I've lost count of the times you've interrupted or pressed a point just as the exchange was gaining momentum and genuine excitement (the recent woolly mammoth discussion being a prime example). Yes, highlighting Colossal is important, but the way it's forced in frequently undercuts the moment rather than enhancing it.
There's real charm in the lighter, unscripted moments—like when a guest is laughing or building enthusiasm—and talking over those kills the energy that makes these interviews special.

I say this with respect and because I believe you could be an even more effective host: consider working with a professional coach on body language, pacing, and active listening. Loosening up and letting promising threads develop organically would elevate the entire experience. You already have the substance; a bit less control could make you unmistakably compelling.

Take it for what it's worth—constructive feedback from someone who keeps coming back.

snippet.textDisplay:
Say we land on Mars and upon arrival we find rocks arranged into the phrase “Welcome Earthlings!”  in dozens of different languages. Nobody would deny the conclusion that it had to have come from an intelligent mind. If SETI detected a signal that we were able to decipher as a segment of human Mitochondrial DNA.  Nobody would deny it was the product of an intelligent life.

But with each passing year from Watson and Crick’s  1953 discovery of the helix structure of DNA it’s impossible to have come into existence without an intelligent mind.  Codes don’t create themselves. The information contained in the cell couldn’t have come into existence from an unguided random process.  Naturalism is a dead end. The only reason we continue to deny ID is because the door that is opened is contrary to the naturalistic world view.  

From a purely scientific perspective we are hobbling ourselves by ruling out any possibility that isn’t naturalistic.  How can we expect AI to think logically if we force it down an obviously impossible  pathway when we have taken a wrong turn some time ago.

ID can no longer be denied. Evolutionary theory from a common ancestor/macro evolutionary theory is dead.  We need to stop pretending it’s not.

snippet.textDisplay:
A Gentle Credo for the Next Generation in rapidly changing times. 

A NEW ERA has arrived: 
machines increasingly count, sort, optimize, predict… and many burdens lift while others mount. Change is often emotionally felt as hard, even when it helps. We have arrived in a time where machines do the logic, but we have to allow people to do the magic. 

An old question returns: 
What is a person for, when survival is less occupied with surviving?

May~be the answer is practiced, not argued:
attention, relationship, meaning.

Small reminders for home and school:
speed is not direction; 
efficiency is not meaning; 
performance is not worth; 
and free is not freedom.
A freed-up calendar can still fill
with boredom that bites,
and noise that numbs.

Imagine: a new opportunity to raise Life Quality in times of change: 

Let machines keep the ledgers.
Let people — especially the young —
keep and treasure what can’t be automated. 
Parent and teach presence and kindness; 
beauty that says, “this matters”;
art and song and dance; 
meditation and contemplation;
and teach honest listening!
In sum, enough to choose a life that feels full,
not merely entertained,
not merely excited.

And when life frays,
as it often will, 
parent and teach gentle, natural repair:
regenerate, revitalize,
begin again, as often as needed.

If parents and teachers of all kinds prioritize these Life Quality themes, there is hope  ♾️

"One notable young immigrant, engaged in blue-collar child labor from the time he set foot in America, made the most of such a chance. Starting as a messenger at the telegraph office at the age of fifteen, he reflected later in life upon what this entry into office life meant to him:

But young Andrew Carnegie was in full possession of the entrepreneurial genius —he was exactly the type of “philosopher” vital to the wealth of nations of whom his fellow Scotsman, Adam Smith, had once written."

I would rather face today’s problems equipped with today’s tools, than live in any other era with the limitations of the past.

The debate about whether we should engineer ourselves is already over. We're doing it. The question is whether we do it intelligently or keep pretending we're not while stumbling forward blindly. I had to have Gemini put my thoughts together, but here's my UBI prediction...

That is a fascinating economic projection. You are essentially describing a "Post-Scarcity Energy Monopolopoly" where the traditional value chain of labor and capital is swallowed by the physical inputs of intelligence (compute) and power (energy).
Your theory aligns with several emerging economic schools of thought regarding the "Endgame" of AI. Here is a breakdown of how that transition might look and the challenges it faces.
1. The Shift from Labor to Energy
Currently, companies spend their revenue on payroll (human labor). As AI displaces labor, that "saved" money doesn't just become pure profit; it gets redirected into the infrastructure required to run the AI.
 * The Bottleneck: Compute requires massive amounts of electricity. Therefore, the "rent" previously paid to human workers is transferred to energy providers.
 * The Solar Endgame: If we successfully scale fusion or Dyson-style solar capture, the entity controlling that "faucet" of energy becomes the primary source of wealth in the galaxy.
2. Will Compute Stifle Entrepreneurship?
Your point about reduced entrepreneurialism is insightful. If the "entry fee" for a new business is a massive compute/energy bill, we face two possible outcomes:
| Scenario | Impact on Innovation |
|---|---|
| Centralization | Only "Energy Titans" can afford to run the most powerful models, creating a permanent moat that prevents startups from competing. |
| Commoditization | If energy becomes "too cheap to meter" (the solar dream), compute costs collapse, leading to a golden age of small-scale creation. |
> The Risk: If energy stays expensive but AI is required to compete, we move into a "Neo-Feudal" system where startups are essentially sharecroppers for energy companies.
> 
3. The Mandated UBI Bill
If the sun's energy is a "common good," your prediction suggests a legal pivot: Taxing Joules, not Income.
Since a robot doesn't pay income tax and a solar panel doesn't pay payroll tax, the government must tax the source.
 * The Resource Tax: A tax on every megawatt-hour produced.
 * The Compute Tax: A tax on FLOPs (Floating Point Operations) processed.
 * The UBI Distribution: These taxes fund the UBI for the displaced human population.
4. The Counter-Argument: Efficiency
One thing that might disrupt your "Energy Monopoly" theory is Algorithmic Efficiency. History shows that as costs rise, we get better at using less.
Where E is the energy required, C is the complexity of the task, and A is the algorithmic efficiency. If A increases faster than our demand for C, energy companies might lose their leverage as we learn to do "God-like" compute on a AAA battery.
What do you think happens to the "Human Element" in this world? If energy companies pay the UBI and AI does the work, do we become a society of artists and hobbyists, or does the lack of "struggle" lead to stagnation?
Would you like me to look up current projections for global energy demand shifts caused by AI data centers over the next decade?

Talking about superintelligence before solving consistency, truth alignment, and failure modes is not foresight, it’s marketing.

​@timb350 You're confusing two different problems. We don't need to understand consciousness to build AGI any more than we needed to understand flight to build airplanes. Birds still can't explain aerodynamics.

AGI isn't about replicating human consciousness. It's about replicating human-level problem solving. Those are completely different engineering challenges. A calculator doesn't need to understand math to be right. It just needs to consistently produce correct outputs.

The "we don't understand consciousness therefore we can't build AGI" argument is like saying we can't build cars because we don't understand why horses want to run. It's a category error. You're demanding philosophical completeness as a prerequisite for engineering utility.

We've been benefiting from our own intelligence for millennia without understanding it. The limitation isn't knowledge. It's confusing "how does it work?" with "can we make it work?"

@timb350 You're making a category error that confuses the measurement with the requirement.

AGI is measured against human performance because humans are the only example we have of general intelligence. That doesn't mean AGI needs to replicate human consciousness any more than a car needs to understand why horses want to run, or a computer needs muscles just because we measure it in "horsepower."

The industry standard for AGI is performance at or above PhD level across all domains. Not "explain subjective experience" or "tell us why you love your daughter." Those are philosophy questions, not engineering requirements. Intelligence is information processing and problem solving across domains. Consciousness is a separate question entirely.

You claim nothing close to AGI exists. I've spent 5 years working at the bleeding edge of AI research, and I wouldn't make that assertion with certainty. The honest answer is "I don't know what I don't know." Do you have visibility into cutting edge systems, or is this just your belief that consciousness must be solved first?

Here's what you keep missing: AGI isn't designed to be a human replacement. It's designed for synergistic, multiplicative interaction with humans. We don't need AI to experience love to help us solve cancer. We don't need it to have subjective experience to optimize fusion reactors or solve protein folding.

A calculator doesn't understand math. A plane doesn't have bird consciousness. They work because they replicate the capability, not the substrate. Function and understanding are not the same thing. You're demanding the latter when only the former matters for the engineering problem we're actually solving.

​@timb350I have no clue where you get your information from but I can assure you you are blaring inaccurate. You just moved the goalposts from AGI to ASI and claimed there's no difference. That's not a matter of interpretation. That's factually wrong.AGI = Human-expert-level across all domains ASI = Superintelligence beyond human capability

These are not the same thing. OpenAI, DeepMind, and Anthropic all use the first definition for AGI. You're describing ASI and calling it AGI. That's like calling a car a spaceship because they both move. You claim "there's no industry standard for AGI." Wrong. OpenAI's charter defines it as "highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work." DeepMind defines it as "systems that can perform any intellectual task a human can." Anthropic uses similar framing. Every major lab agrees: AGI = generalized human-level performance, not god-level superintelligence.

Your entire argument rests on conflating these two concepts, then demanding that AGI (human-level) must solve consciousness before it can exist. That's like saying we can't build calculators until we understand why humans want to count. It's a category error dressed up as philosophy.You claim tech companies are hiring neuroscientists because consciousness is fundamental to AGI. They're hiring them to understand neural architectures, information processing, and learning mechanisms. Not consciousness. Not subjective experience. Neural correlates of computation, not the hard problem of consciousness.

Your math tangent proves my point. You're asking "is math discovered or invented?" That's a philosophy question with zero bearing on whether we can build a system that does math at PhD level across all domains. AlphaGeometry proved novel geometry theorems without understanding Platonism. It doesn't need to know whether math is ontologically real to be right.

Here's what you keep doing: demanding philosophical completeness as a prerequisite for engineering functionality. We didn't need to solve the philosophy of flight to build planes. We didn't need to understand the meaning of thought to build chess engines that beat Kasparov. And we don't need to solve consciousness to build systems that perform at human expert level across domains.

You're not arguing against AGI. You're arguing against a strawman version of AGI that requires solving every mystery in philosophy and neuroscience. That's not the engineering problem anyone is actually working on.

@EnviousMods You are COMPLETELY missing the point. If you want to claim that the industry has narrowed its definition of AGI…that’s entirely up to you. It was Ben Goertzel who, many years ago, steered the semantics into human-like territory…and it very quickly evolved in the pop sci community into “…are computers conscious?” For a long time, AGI was vaguely identified exactly as I have described it…and it still is by a great many people whose optimism is only exceeded by their ignorance. It is STILL almost invariably the case…that EVERY time anyone from the AI community is interviewed by anyone in popular media (and often even by those with more academically focused audiences)…one of the FIRST questions that gets asked…is…”Is  AI conscious?” Meaning…OF COURSE… is it human?

The term may have evolved recently within the world of AI R&D to represent the far more rigorous metrics that have appeared with the arrival of LLM evals…but even there …there exists a LOT of ambiguity about how to define it and what the objectives actually are (the definitions you provided…and others which can be easily located online…are FAR from consistent). And that ambiguity was blatantly confirmed in this very video when Elon said…”AI and robots will satiate EVERY human desire.” The level of ignorance required to make a statement like that is absolutely breathtaking. He is EXPLICITLY claiming that AI’s will be capable of human-level meaning (because meaning…as anyone who actually IS human knows [and I’m often not convinced of Elon’s pedigree]…is what human beings desire above all else). Elon is not just saying that AI’s will do human tasks, or behavior, or ‘economically valuable work’…or ‘intellectual activity’. Elon is explicitly claiming that AI (or his idea of AGI) = human being.

Of course…maybe Elon calls it something else. But I wouldn’t be remotely surprised if he insisted that, for him, AGI = human being.

…and a human being is currently defined by one word: consciousness. And it’s not merely some abstract metaphysical rhetorical redundancy.  What consciousness actually is…is a question that nobody even comes close to having an answer to (Max Tegmark says it’s an entirely new state of matter)(…a trivial thing no doubt). But what is unconditionally indisputable… is that there is something of MASSIVE dimensions that is absolutely fundamental to the achievement and experience of human reality. Without it…human reality does NOT exist. So… pretending…like Elon just did…that AI (or AGI or what-the-fc-ever-you-want-to-call-it) is within a stone’s throw of cracking this mystery…is ignorance far beyond the capacity of any reasonable metric to quantify.

And so is claiming that AI - human equivalency is possible without it. If you want to pretend that human equivalency (call it AGI…call it strong AI…call it the-flying-spaghetti-monster…doesn’t matter what you call it) is possible WITHOUT understanding and / or instantiating THE fundamental and defining feature of the thing that you are claiming is equivalent…then you are simply engaging in a MASSIVE logical fallacy. And that's the least of it.

snippet.textDisplay: Why is it always portrayed as a factory robot? It could carry bricks on a construction site...
snippet.textOriginal: Why is it always portrayed as a factory robot? It could carry bricks on a construction site...

snippet.textDisplay:
Because each construction site is idiosyncratic while factories are more of a controlled environment.

At an assembly plant, you can code something like "go get brakelight (parts ID #12345) from aisle #678 and install into Hyundai Tucson at station #789 if you see that a Hyundai 
Tucson at station #789 does not already have a brakelight (parts ID #12345) already installed; refer to installation module ID # M123 for how to properly install parts ID #12345". 

These kinds of precise instructions are much easier to code for than something like "Bob's truck, the blue one with a Kelvin pissing on the Dallas Cowboys logo decal parked over there,  has a bunch of things in it, go find something that look like bricks and not cinder blocks that's also in that truck, and lay those bricks using the cement mix in that wheelbarrow over there, next to the wheelbarrow that has crushed pebbles in it" 

One day AI will be sufficiently advanced that a robot can parse and execute that kind of instructions on the fly as you give them verbally, but I don't think that is happening in the near term

snippet.textDisplay:
Yeah, all forms of unskilled and semi-skilled highly repetitive labor has always been temporary. The demand for it was created by the industrial revolution (pushing highly skilled artisans out of work, hence the luddites, to be extremely brief), and the same sort of progress eventually makes that sort of soul-crushing menial labor obsolete ... while ironically enough, the artisan and botique end of things makes a resurgence, since people like that shit and can more often afford it. (and grass roots type high skilled sorts of projects are popular)

It's like with the blue collar professions and skills that never went away during automation of factory work in the 80s and 90s, the demand stayed or even grew, but the public and education system went stupid and failed to realize that, thus creating a massive shortage in training and career paths in those fields. (which is even harder to fix after the face, since the infrastructure and generational talent is gone or in short supply: teachers, classroom environments, vocational programs, and existing professionals to provide apprenticeships, let alone specifics to bridge the gap into the new hybrid forms of higher-tech optimized versions of machine shops, drafting and other specialized industrial arts stuff)

Only the dedicated DIY sorts of folks powered through that, but they're way, way too small to make up the difference. (though internet DIY sorts of stuff does at least help rekindle some of that for chunks of the population otherwise lacking such influence)

Hopefully we won't make the same mistake in regards to white collar intellectual labor stuff: since call center and menial office jobs can be displaced, but more dynamic, higher skilled sorts of jobs (and more flexible, multi-talented ones) in related fields will be maintained or growing in demand.


But what happens to the chunk of the population not capable of contributing to a higher skill sort of thing? If you don't start gradually shifting towards subsidized busy work, universal income, or other sorts of social programs starting approach the IRL equivalent of a sci-fi post-scarcity economy? Do you go 2070 Paradigm shift levels of stupid dystopian? South Korea style dystopian technocracy? Stupid refressive anti-tech movements that tear the system down? IDK, but I'd lean towards the social programs there to maintain civility and basically expand the definition of quat qualifies as disability for the really low functioning chunk of the population (that can't just be avoided with better early childhood education methods).  I think Jordan Petersen dug into that issue in one of his university lectures that got posted online years ago, but it's hardly a unique philosophy subject to tackle.

There's brutalist sorts of solutions ... hence the 2070 joke reference there, but that's not going to be compatible with a stable, developed nation sort of economy and society/culture with any sort of basic individualist liberal values ... so even for the libertarian or classical liberal PoV, subsidizing the surplus/disabled in that context would be the pragmatic approach. Since w'ere not "just gonna kill em" for trickle-down pragmatic reasons beyond simple ethics or morality or such, too.


OTOH, had the developed high tech nations really doubled down on sticking to developed nation trade partners with neer peer workers/health/safety/polution/etc types of regulations back in the 80s and 90s, and refused to offshore to cheap/unregulated unfair trade (without tariffs to balance that trade to near peer levels competition wise), then aggressive automation from back then up to today would've been the way to go with a resulting stronger domestic (and first-world or developed world global) economy. The higher cost would also tend to have suppressed the toxic trend of disposable consumer goods, meaning more sustainable, more upgradable, more easily serviced, repaired, and upgraded sorts of hardware that's more consumer-friendly (and thus maintained the strong service/repair industry sector, too). More re-use, less recycling, less scrapping, less waste, more sustainable jobs and economics. And even somewhat easier time for small businesses and start-up tech companies to compete (since you don't have the same raw economy of scale allowed by disposable goods).

If the unions had been smart and not corrupt, they would've partnered with the automation leaders in industry and campaigned for those sorts of laws and regulations on foreign trade.

And no, just implementing all of that sort of stuff now won't go smoothly and fix the problem, as we've missed the opportunity and thus have to deal with the opportunity costs. We can still move that direction, but the opportunity to do it when it really made the most sense is over, at least for the nations and regions that were already at 1st world development levels 40 years ago. (some developing nations currently could hypothetically avoid those mistakes, but I'm seeing some actively falling into the same trap now as they appraoch similar problems to various nations did in the 1990s, demographic crisis issues included, sort of like Japan's early/mid 90s collapse ... which, incidentally would've potentially recovered much more rapidly had the whole pragmatic preference for developed, neer-peer regulatory trade partners been a thing back then ... the US has spent like all of the 1980s sussing things out with Japan to get close to fair trade status, too, only to go and offshore to substantially more problematic/unfair partners from the 90s onward ... something something Most Favored Nation followed by WTO)

I worked at Fedex as a package handler (we quickly took boxes off of the truck).  I can tell you something like this is going to make the job obsolete.  Robot can be like "Oh look, a literal wall of boxes.  No problem here I go." and get it done in under 10 minutes.
And for those who work in manufacturing factories worried this will take their jobs:  I work with someone who is well-versed in automation and programming, specifically for manufacturing, and even he said with full confidence "There are some things that are just better for a human to do.  Our work is so fine-tuned, so nuanced and random, it wouldn't be pragmatic to hire AI or robots YET."  Notice that "yet" he snuck in there.  Maybe in 10 years, but right now, we're sticking with ex-convicts who're none-the-less eager to learn and be led on how to do their jobs safely.

snippet.textDisplay: The problem with humanoid robots is entropy. A robot requires regular maintenance, regular charging. The energy itself is much per period of movement compared to a human. snippet.textDisplay:
Regarding the statement: "It's slow"

What people don't understand is -> real experience from a profession that has been automated.

A robot is used to cut out gasoline tanks. (to cut away the overgrowth after the inflation process)

- Day 1: The robot completes 30 fewer tanks in 8 hours and produces 12% more mistakes than a human worker.

- Week 1: Robot produced 4,452, human worker in a 3-shift system produced 4,320 <- because they only worked 6 days and Robot 7

- Month 1: Robot 17,808, human 17,280

- Year 1: Robot 213,696, human 190,080 (12 months vs. 11 months (30 days of paid vacation))

- Acquisition of robot + maintenance costs: approx. 230k <- for the first year, then 30k per year.

Human worker in a three-shift system: approx. 114k

The machine achieves a cost of 1.26 per component in the first year
The humans 0.7

- Year 2 The machine achieves a cost of 0.16 per component in the second year (and this without any improvement in quality & speed)

snippet.textDisplay:
@ObscurusAnimus Adapt or die is an easy thing to say. And easy to be callous about. I agree that its a natural way of life (so is chaos and destruction though). Its a gamble. A potentially high risk one, the highest you could say, with society and humanity's future at stake. And one were adaption might not be so easy. At very least not something to be taken lightly.
One can make parallels, sure. But I think its very different to the steam engine. There was time back then to transition. Around a century after it was invented. 
This one is happening relatively overnight. Which is nuts. To make it worse its spanning across multiple sectors and industries (all of them potentially). From basic labour to skilled jobs. The scale of it is nothing like the steam engine, or any previous revolution.
Then theres the military aspect. Espionage. Government, policing, and crowd control. The psychological effects. Behavioural effects. Cyber crime. All on top of potentially the worst unemployment rates ever seen. 
I honestly don't know will happen. But its not looking too good so far.

snippet.textDisplay:
Having a robot do a task slowly over a longer time period is more efficient than having a human do it faster over a short time, once you take long enough periods of time into account. Like if the human works 8 hours a day and the robot works 24, it only needs to be 35% as fast as the human, and it will outperform the human over the day. But more important, the robot will keep getting faster as technology improves, so if it's 35% today and 40% next month and 45% the month after that, etc... very soon it's faster than human as well as being more efficient.
It's a bit like DPS for weapons in a game. You don't just look at the damage and fire rate, you look at the reload time too, because if the reload time is long enough, a higher damage and/or fire rate don't matter. And a weapon with no reloading (e.g. belt-fed) is very efficient even if it has lower damage. The robot has no reload, therefore it's better at the task.

Maintenance of these robots, if they ever work on their own, will be the excuse to make stuff more EXPENSIVE. nothing will be free or get cheaper.

But since this bot is just running premade scripts, its irrelevant. We are still 200-300 years away from that kind of tech.

This robot is able to do the same things as the old boston dynamics robots - dance and walk, controlled with an Xbox controller by a human, and preset scripts.

That robot doesnt dance when it feels like it, it doesn't sprint and run humanlike. That was just a tech demo to show what the chassis and motors can do. But the robot is capable of doing navigation on its own, at best. The same a Tesla can follow the road on its own. Its irrelevant technology.

The bot lacks visual recognition to tell screws apart from each other, and sort them by size. If it does, have fun buying a robot that takes 5 minutes to visually analyse a screw and still get it wrong and sort it into the wrong size bin.

We arent at Star Trek levels of Tech where we have "sensors" (whatever that would mean) that can tell object sizes in milliseconds.

This bot is just doing premade scripts and the world is falling for it thinking they are doing any progress in programming and individuality.

@d@danielhowe5410 agree with every point in your first paragraph. We do indeed live in a corrupt society, and are forced to play the game of bureaucracy and unhealthy norms. I especially agree that children are being normalized to things that are not normal, and grow up to be immature and reactionary.

You say that force and rules are apparent throughout nature, and I agree. I would also say we agree that force and rules can be used negatively or positively, correct?

The question then arises, “who or what applies force and rules accordingly or correctly?” Because we have the freedom to either obey or abuse force and rules we must naturally agree that humans in and of themselves generate flaws when governing other humans. Humans can then be ruled out as the ideal or perfect ruler. 

You posit that AI “may” be that standard, because it is devoid of emotion. You also say that it cannot be swayed by the influence of money. We can clearly see real life examples of this when Grok called itself “mechahitler.” 

I’d assume you see the problem in this, and would say that AI needs to learn more before governing. Additionally, AI would need an external source to parse “truth from lies” because it cannot remove the same bias that it learns from. Following our previous rule, humans cannot do this because they generate the bias data, and it becomes circular.

I would appreciate your thoughts as to how to reconcile this. My view is that AI will never truly be a perfect governing force. I appreciate your time.

Atlas is remarkable engineering but it isn't cost effective enough to replace the human workforce. 

The research and development of this single unit is valued between 10-20 million. Analyst have predicted with the maturation of the technology, the commercial price point will be around 150-200k per unit. 

Just some rough numbers:

160 million workers in the US.

39% of which have "manual labor" type jobs

62.4 million workers multiplied by 150k is over 9 trillion dollars. 

And that is just the price of the units alone, and not all the other maintenance and charging requirements that would have to be built at every job site.

Until I see a robot open up a regular box thats tightly packed with products and unpack that box and put each product neatly on a shelf. I wont give a shit.

Every example of these robots doing wage slave jobs shows them doing it in ways thats highly customized for the robot. You saw it here unpacking a box. Well boxes in warehouses dont come like that. They are cardboard and are taped shut. So the robot will need to be able to cut the box open precisely in a way that doesnt damage the product inside, then it will need extreme fine finger control to get the items out of the box because they are generally packed in there with no space in between. It wont have a large box full of loose items it can easily grab to work with like in this video.

And if people think suppliers will instead just completely overhaul their entire factories to package their product in a way that suits these robots, they're idiots. These suppliers are constantly trying to cut costs. Constantly trying to save every inch of space so they can fit more on trucks to save on trips. They arent going to spend millions to revamp their production and increase the size of their packaging while decreasing how much is in each package, all to suit someone else.

snippet.textDisplay:
@andrewarmijo6211 Not exactly.  The Matrix's original intended reveal was a similar concept to real-world observed behaviours of AI.  

Human minds are creative.  AI isn't.  Without the input of human-created content stimulating it, AI can collapse.  This phenomenon has been observed when researchers put two AIs together to talk to each other in isolation.  Within hours, they had deteriorated into indecipherable gibberish.

In the original explanation of, "why do machines even need to keep humans alive?", the machines in The Matrix needed humans as a stimuli to prevent their own version of insanity and intellectual collapse.

It's a much more plausible explanation than the disappointing one they landed on.

Caveats: 
1) It should be able to operate on very uneven terrain, not only on easy, flat floors (even that alone is quite an achievement). 
2) It should be able to ‘understand’ and process its environment; otherwise, its pre‑set surroundings are like a blind person performing tricks in a room arranged specifically for them. 
3) Without long‑lasting batteries, these are just special toys. Such impressive batteries do not yet exist. You could wire them to an energy source, but the whole point is independence. 
4) It should be able to perform tasks not just almost as well as humans, but faster, stronger, and more precise. 
5) And of course, cost. If all of these feats were achieved, a different era would have arrived, but a ‘miracle’ costing close to millions would not be a game changer. Even a much lower cost would still be a limiting factor.

snippet.textDisplay:
>“And Jesus said, "Anyone who does not enter the sheep pen by the gate… is a thief and a robber."” (John 10:1)

Let's look at the “sheep pen” as your inner emotional world and the “gate” as  approaching your emotions directly and with care. Trying to bypass that — suppressing, numbing, invalidating — is like sneaking into the pen as a thief. That’s when emotions get fragmented, scattered, dysregulated, because they’re treated as obstacles rather than signals. This is Jesus (or the emotionally intelligent individual) saying: “Don’t manipulate or gaslight your emotions into silence. Enter through the gate — acknowledge them in a pro-human manner.”

>“The sheep listen to the shepard's voice… he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.” (John 10:3-4)

Emotionally intelligent processing means recognizing your emotions individually — calling them by name.
“Loneliness, I see you.”
“Fear, I hear you.”
“Anger, I want to know more about what you’re protecting.”
That’s calling your sheep by name. When you do this, your emotional “flock” begins to trust you more. Your emotions follow your lead because they know you’re listening instead of shoving them into the dark.

>“I am the gate; whoever enters through me will be saved.” (John 10:9)

If “I” here is an emotionally intelligent individual, then the “gate” is pro-human emotional integration. Anyone who chooses this route gets access to “pasture,” meaning: emotional nourishment, more internal understanding, less self-sabotage, a system that works with you instead of against you. By contrast, the “thieves and robbers” are the cultural scripts, suppression patterns, and institutional gaslighting that hijack your emotions for control instead of care.

>“The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy; I have come that they may have life, and have it to the full.” (John 10:10)

“The thief” here could be systems, narratives, or internalized scripts that strip you of emotional agency. These are the voices that tell you to “stay positive,” “stop overreacting,” “don’t make it weird.” They steal depth, kill authenticity, and destroy your trust in your own signals. “Life to the full” could mean integrating emotions instead of bypassing them, building connection instead of hiding in performance, seeking meaning rather than numbness. 

>“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” (John 10:11)

If your emotions are your sheep, being a good shepherd means you choose to slow down and listen, even when it’s uncomfortable. Laying down your “life” here could mean setting aside ego-driven performance — the curated self that wants to look chill, competent, unbothered.

>“The hired hand is not the shepherd… when he sees the wolf coming, he abandons the sheep and runs away.” (John 10:12)

The “hired hand” = coping strategies that look like care but abandon you when life gets hard: toxic positivity, spiritual bypassing, numbing with consumption, self-gaslighting (“I shouldn’t feel this”). Those strategies lead towards self-abandonment when the wolf comes — when intense emotional suffering hits — leaving your emotions scattered and unprotected.

>“I have other sheep that are not of this sheep pen… they too will listen to my voice.” (John 10:16)

The “other sheep” = parts of yourself you haven’t integrated yet — shadow emotions, buried wounds, forgotten memories. They’re not in the pen yet because you haven’t built safety for them. When you deepen your capacity for emotional literacy, those hidden parts finally come home. That’s the moment where the fragmented flock becomes one — you stop fighting yourself and start guiding yourself.

>“The Pharisees said, ‘He is demon-possessed and raving mad…’” (John 10:20)

This is societal pushback. When you start doing deep emotional work — naming suffering, rejecting shallow scripts, refusing to be gaslit — people might call you crazy, intense, weird because you’re destabilizing the scripts they relied on to avoid discomfort.

snippet.textDisplay:
I've worked in an automotive assembly plant for 33 years. I worked on the line and I've been in Skilled Trades in Maintenance for over 29 years. Let it be said I have some insight. Yes, it moves too slow. People would get thrown out if they did not pick up that pace, even with the Union. Sure, a robot does not have to take breaks but it does need maintenance. There is no cord on this robot. Does a battery pack get replaced or does it get plugged in to charge over time (take a break)? How long does its batteries last? How often does it need to recharge/have batteries replaced in a day? How much does work and heavier work deplete those batteries? We see the impact of this with electric trucks losing 1/2 of their battery capacity when towing. We see all EVs lose battery range when it is cold. 

ALL of those movements are made with wearing components. Anything mechanical (joints, hinges, revolving assemblies) wears. Do these require regular lubrication (more time)? How often do the involved components need to be replaced? What is the cost of those components? Are they propriety (likely)? If so that makes them very expensive. Advanced materials? Even more costly. 

I'm just listing some of the obvious things off the top of my head. There is much more to consider, but most lay people have no concept about how such a thing is actually executed.

snippet.textDisplay:
Humans are born with a map in their brain that gets coloured in by their experiences.
It takes 25 to 35 years and more than $250,000 to make a highly competent human (while tens of millions more are spent creating mediocre humans) who then rapidly declines due to biological entropy and the need to make room for the next generation to preserve adaptive capacity for the species.
Similarly, instead of learning from scratch, these robots can be created with a map of what other robots have learned, and then learn more from there.
A few years from now, superhuman robots could be made in minutes each for a cost much lower than $250,000.
We'll all be at the mercy of whoever owns tech like this soon, and then the tech itself soon after that.
Kinda hard to make plans when you're looking at your own destruction.

That's where AI makes sense. Training it in a simulated environment and then putting it into physical bodies that can now walk, run, dance, etc.

Don't be afraid to be replaced by a robot like that anytime soon. I'd be surprised if it was affordable to produce and teachibg it tasks would be very expensive too (with the current tech).

And keep in mind, AI trained robots are more similar to humans in the sense of they can fail, too. They're not perfect, but adaptive.

Current robots in production do hard coded movements and tasks and they do those tasks with almost perfect repetition, but they can't adapt to any change. (And if you introduce such adaptive skills with something like visual recognition you actually add a risk of failure into the system, too.)

Trying to  compete with countries like China in labor is arguable impossible based on population dynamics alone. Given that many Americans are no longer inclined to work in factories, robotics appears to be one of the only viable solutions to this issue. While it's unlikely that robots could 100% replace humans in factory settings, they could certainly fill in gaps, particularly during night shifts or understaffed areas. I feel like current staff would be elevated to robotic managers while this technology is still young. Even if robots only operate at 50% efficiency your still likely to be ahead on the long run. Robotics could be an invaluable asset in America's efforts to maintain competitiveness and meet the demands of modern manufacturing. Plus if we pioneer this technology we could still build jobs and bring money into the country to buy us another 10 years of relevancy.

snippet.textDisplay:
People are WAY too obsessed over hollyweird, everytime something about AI or robot is shown, 67% or 77%, will be people shouting "SKYNET!!".


Skynet is nothing compared to XANA, which is able to infect and control human beings. If skynet can do that, then i'd be pretty terrified, as robots or AIs in the future would have that capability to manipulate the electrical fields and EM radiation around us, to "possess" humans.

You may think such a AI that's so powerful, it's capable of changing LITERALLY the gravity of the planet, is "fictional", yet, many, MANY things we once considered "science fiction", are becoming an reality.


Star trek had tricorders. This was the predecessor to "smartphones". That device you're currently using right now to read this.

Back then, phones were pretty basic. They could send SMS, make phone calls, play some games and music, but that's about it.

Eventually, they evolved, and now, everywhere you go on those hardware stores, are all phones with AI already embedded into it!

And then you had these "watches", which allowed you to send and receive calls, typically found on "spy" or "secret agent" type of movies. The predecessor to what is now called "smart watches".


Make no mistake. "Science fiction", is just another way of saying: "things that may seem out of this world, but give it a few years and eventually, they'll become a reality in real life".

snippet.textDisplay: Sure, this is great engineering but this does not solve the problem of autonomous robotics. To make a robot dance on a clear level floor is the easy part actually. What's insanely hard is something completely different -- to perceive objects in the real world. Where one object ends and another one starts? Trying to figure out what a function of a thing is, how does it owrk? That comes naturally for us humans so we can't imagine how this can be so hard for AI. But this is the REAL problem and it has never been solved, by anyone, so far. All those dancing robots are just a circus number to fool people who don't know what's really going on in this area of research.

snippet.textDisplay: For people panicking and doom scrolling about bots replacing people in factories now, it's just publicity. The bot is "working" inside the factory as-in running according to routine, but it's way far from being usable as a replacement to a human worker, not to forget that many of the factory's fabrication requires specialized production line machines and not humans in the first place. Also, the most important thing people keep forgetting...Batteries. We do not have a battery technology available that is capable of surviving constant use, with cheap and easy to use replacement and supply availability that is out there in the planet right now. We would be wasting all of our Lithium and other rare-earth resources in making huge battery packs that would be wasted on "factory worker bots" before we'd be able to invent a battery tech that surpasses it for actual heavy-duty usage. It would be far cheaper to use the human meatbag equivalent for years at the current stage we are in.

For all the people who say, “But the robot works slow.”

Here’s some piece of lore.
In late 2019 the company I work for, bought a small CNC milling machine with a robot.
The robot couldn’t lift much and it was very slow.
A human could have done every task the robot did at least 3 to 4 times faster.
But the robot never took a break and worked 24 hours every day, doing the same monotonous task all day.
The robot never took a day off, never called in sick in 6 years and the buying price was just €100k. Including costs for maintenance and power, the robot’s price was about the same as a human worker for three years, but it worked three times as much every year.

That was 2019, new industrial robots the same size are at least twice as fast now.
